messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm trying to interpret the results on phylogenetic signal of my ulnar shape data. First, Kmult = 0.90 (p = 0.0001) which means that closely related species show a similar distal ulnar shape, though slightly less than expected under a BM model of evolution, despite the large effect size (4.08). But K on the first component was quite large (1.79, p = 0.001) so Kmult = 0.90 is not a weak phylogenetic signal (but concentrated in some but not all variables of the original data).

When I investigate phylogenetic signal along the components of a phyPCA and PACA, I find the following results:
- phyPCA comp 1: K = 0.58 (p = 0.04)
- phyPCA comp 2: K = 1.60 (p = 0.001)
- phyPCA comp 3: K = 0.58 (p = 0.06)

- PACA comp 1: K = 0.66 (p = 0.03)
- PACA comp 2: K = 2.14 (p = 0.001)
- PACA comp 3: K = 1.03 (p = 0.009)

I would have expected that the phylogenetic signal in the first component of PACA to be larger because PACA normally aligns with phylogenetic signal. The phylogenetic signal on the phyPCA is low for the first component which is expected as it is mostly independent of phylogenetic signal. Additionally, the shape variations described along the second component are the same for both phyPCA and PACA (a wider ulnar head + larger distal projection), and the phylogenetic signal is the highest in this second component. Does the larger phylogenetic signal along the second component mean that these shape variations are more aligned with phylogeny than those on the first component?

When looking at the summary of both the phyPCA and PACA, this is the outcome (see image attached). I'm also not sure how I need to interpret these results, even after reading various publications (e.g. the RV, or what this information can tell me about the ancestors, ...).

Thanks for your help! I really appreciate it.

Marie.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Marie,

Your results sure are challenging!  I’m not sure I can help, but I’ll start with the things that are obvious.

PACA (and to a certain extent, PCA) is like 2B-PLS, maximizing covariance between two matrices.  The data are found in the first matrix and the second matrix is the covariance matrix based on phylogenetic covartiances.  (For PCA, the second matrix is an identity matrix.)  So let’s start with the stats that are more naïve regarding phylogenetic signal.  The singular values are like the square root of eigenvalues in PCA, explaining the component strength of association.  One can add up the squared singular values and divide by the single squared values for each component to get a percentage of the overall co-variation between matrices expressed by each component.  You can see that the first component explains 96.8% of the overall covariation, which is quite impressive.  However, what if there is little overall covariation between matrices?  Would 96.8% of practically nothing be all that impressive?  The RV explains that covariation as portion of the joint variation between matrices (more like a portion of variance).  It is like a squared correlation coefficient, or a coefficient of determination. The first component explains 63.7% of the joint variation, which is also impressive.  The second 1.2%, the third 0.2%, etc.  So, the analysis is doing what it is supposed to do, maximizing covariation between the two matrices in the first dimension.

However, when looking at the dispersion among points after projecting data on components, there is more dispersion among points on the second component, whether looking at tips or ancestors, which is why K is probably larger on the second component.  It is difficult to picture a PAC plot in my mind that shows the phylogeny most aligned with the first PAC but more dispersion on the second PAC.  Maybe there is a tree that has two subclades, split from a really deep node but not much morphological difference between these subclades compared to within them, even though the branch lengths separating species within subclades are small.  This is a guess — it’s hard to visualize — but I believe you might have an interesting tree?

Maybe if you could provide an illustration of your tree, along with PC and PAC plots, it would be easier to offer an explanation.  It is truly bizarre that your first PAC explains so much of the covariation with your data set but more dispersion is found along the second component.  I just cannot reconcile this with hypothetical mental pictures.

Best,
Mike

Are you suggesting for point #1 that your analysis was at the individual level and for #2 and #3 your analyses were at the species level (species means)?  If so, there is no really large problem.  What you have learned is that species tend to have divergent allometries, requiring allometry to be analyzed within-species.  There is no way to do a PGLS-type analysis that compares species means, accounting for allometry at a species level, based on disparate within-species allometries.  You can perform a species-level allometry analysis by finding species shape means and species size means, using these size means as a covariate in procD.pgls.  Just do not include species in your model.  But you would do this knowing that at the individual level, species have different allometries, so within- and among-species analyses are probably both needed.

Hope that helps.

Mike

messages.subject: Is ProcD.lm analyzing one landmark at a time?
messages.subject_clean: Is ProcD.lm analyzing one landmark at a time?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

The Procrustes regression is performed in geomorph through the procD.lm function. I noted that the regression coefficients obtained for each coordinate of each landmark using ProcD.lm is the same as extracting that coordinate value and obtaining regression coefficients using lm().

For example:
data(plethodon)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land) #GPA-alignment
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, site = plethodon$site, species = plethodon$species)
fit1 <- procD.lm(coords ~ species, + data = gdf, iter = 999, turbo = TRUE, + RRPP = TRUE)

fit1$coefficients shows that the intercept and regression coefficients for x-coordinate of landmark 1 is 0.15972601 and -0.01478733, which are the same as obtained using lm(coorded[,1] ~ gdf$species)$coefficients.

There has been the concensus in GMM that landmarks cannot be analyzed one at a time. However, what the procD.lm does, in terms of regression coefficient estimation (without regard to statistical inference of significance) seems no different from using lm() multiple times. This means procD.lm is merely giving all separately estimated regression coefficients at once, which is no different from using lm() multiple times.

Having realized this issue, I am confused as to how I could be confident in saying that I am not analyzing one lanmdark at a time when using procD.lm, such as shape on the continuous variable of age. I still believe procD.lm is the method of choice when indicated, but I am curious to learn how to eschew the potential pitfall of analyzing landmarks one at a time when using procD.lm. Perhaps examples of when one makes such a mistake while using procD.lm and when one doesn't while using procD.lm would help clarify.

Thank you.

Best regards,
Kieran

messages.body_plain:
Kieran,

Please consult a basic multivariate textbook.  This particular observation (that the regression coefficients column by column in multivariate regression happen to be the same as those of each variable treated individually) is a mathematical outcome of the procedure: it is not unique to procD.lm or any other software implementation.  Nor does it invalidate use of ANOVA/regression in shape analysis. What matters in this case is that the overall covariation between the overall shape and the explanatory variable is summarized across the entire multivariate space. SS, MS, F etc. are not obtained dimension by dimension.

The recommendation you mentioned: ‘don’t interpret/analyze landmarks one at a time’ issue is regarding any attempt to interpret patterns of variation or covariation one landmark at a time. As was shown by Rohlf and Slice 1990, the actual variation/covariation landmark by landmark is influenced by the superimposition; rendering such a variable by variable analysis inappropriate (based on current approaches).  However, that is not what is done in multivariate regression. While the regression parameters are the same as if obtained individually, the overall summary of variation/covariation of the single m-regression is not.

As an example, try fitting a linear model for your multivariate regression in base-R. Then use ‘summary’ of that fit. One will obtain an analysis variable by variable: not what one wishes to do.  Then, use ‘summary(manova…)’ of that fit. This is the proper multivariate analysis.

Example below.

###

library(geomorph)

data("plethodon")

Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)

size <- log(Y.gpa$Csize)

shape <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords)$x

fit <- lm(shape~size)

#This performs the analysis variable by variable, and is incorrect

summary(fit)

#this is the multivariate analysis

summary(manova(fit))

In case there could be some remaining confusion for observers of this thread, I would like to add an addendum to Dean’s example.  First, I wish to address Kieran’s comment, "There has been the concensus in GMM that landmarks cannot be analyzed one at a time. However, what the procD.lm does, in terms of regression coefficient estimation (without regard to statistical inference of significance) seems no different from using lm() multiple times.”  This sentence answers itself, as analysis and estimation are different things.  The reason procD.lm and lm do not differ in the coefficients they estimate is because they both use least-squares estimation, which is not different if used variable by variable or for a set of variables.  Analysis starts after estimation is completed, by applying probabilities to estimates, under a null hypothesis.

Again, here is Dean’s example:

###
library(geomorph)
data("plethodon")
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)
size <- log(Y.gpa$Csize)
shape <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords)$x

fit <- lm(shape~size)

#This performs the analysis variable by variable, and is incorrect
summary(fit)

#this is the multivariate analysis
summary(manova(fit))

As Dean notes, the summary(fit) part performs multiple tests, PC by PC (rather than landmark by landmark, but the point is the same).  Before analysis, let’s compare what estimation does.

Kieran,

A few points here:

1: I would not use PCs as variables in an actual empirical study. Instead I would use the set of Procrustes-aligned coordinates

2: Yes, use of all PC scores OR use of Procrustes coordinates will yield identical statistical results IF one uses robust statistical approaches/permutations, etc.

3: However, parametric implementations of MANOVA/Regression will fail to work on the full set of Procrustes aligned residuals, because they contain redundant dimensions due to translation, rotation, scale. That means the resulting covariance matrices derived from them are singular, and thus at the model evaluation step where inverses of covariance matrices are needed, the algebra attempts to divide by zero, which obviously leads to undesirable outcomes!

My example was to show you the fact that separate analyses one variable at a time is not the same as using all variables at once. But if you look carefully at my code, I used the parametric version of linear models ‘lm’ to show the point (it was simply a bit more expedient in code to do so).  By contrast, if I had attempted that using the full set of Procrustes residuals, my example would have failed to run.  (Note: ProcD.lm will not have this problem because it evaluates the model using permutations, not parametric distributions. But that also means the point of the earlier post would be lost).

Again I encourage a careful reading of the underlying theoretical papers and textbooks of the field, and of multivariate statistics. These are issues we have resolved several decades ago. For one to be a competent user and practitioner of morphometrics today, one really does need to put in the literature work to understand what one is doing with these software packages.

Dean

In fact, in some cases one could start to find results that are increasingly bad, as landmarks slide past each other, and variance among configurations is minimized by finding morphological impossibilities.  This is under-appreciated area of research in need of more theoretical development!  However, one could empirically explore for an optimal number of iterations (minimize variance while retaining morphological reasonableness).

>From a practical perspective, Dean’s points are spot on.  It does not matter if you use Procrustes coordinates or the full set of PC scores for Procrustes ANOVA.  If performing MANOVA, then using only the PCs that have non-zero eigenvalues is essential, and a case could be made that using only a portion of the PCs that explain, e.g., 98 or 99% of the variation might be better to avoid problems with statistics that find the determinant of ill-conditioned matrices.  This is an ad hoc solution similar to what Miriam was noting, statistical limitations, not in general but with some data sets.  I’ll add two more considerations. First, if one wishes to transform a reference configuration to a target configuration based on predicted shape changes by a linear model, Procrustes coordinates are required.  This would not work with PC scores.  Second, if one has a situation where a measure of model likelihood is needed, PC scores will be in order, especially if one has many sliding landmarks (in which case some arbitrary cut-off of the number of PCs is also probably needed).  This is related to the MANOVA concern, but maybe not for statistical tests (rather for comparing models with a model selection criterion).

If one is a coder, when to use coordinates or PCs might be determined by one’s need for proficiency.  For example, the default in procD.lm is turbo = TRUE.  One would choose this is they are not worried about estimating coefficients in every RRPP permutation (which requires coordinates).  In this case, PCs are used, because they are always fewer in number than the coordinates, so thousands of permutations could be performed in less time and with less burden on computer memory.  “This sounds like hair-splitting!” might say the person who has not had to worry about users hitting computational ceilings with their large, complex data sets.

Cheers!
Mike

Yiru

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] on the use of separate GPAs for modularity and integration tests

messages.body_plain:
> > Is there a way to include a single landmark in multiple modules or do I need to make some decisions about what landmarks to assign to a single module?

I am really happy this question was asked!  I am happy because it leads to a similar topic that I think needs to be discussed.  If you wish to avoid a soapbox moment from me, please stop reading now.

In his 2019 paper, Cardini advocated for performing separate GPAs on modules before testing for modularity or integration, to reduce the risk of spurious integration and modularity signals in shape data, that seems to arise from GPA.  (I would posit that covariances that suggest modularity or integration probably have a physical spatial signal that is not purely induced by GPA but following this topic would be a digression from the present one.)  It was a convenience in the examples considered that landmarks fell into separate modules but like Madlen’s example, maybe landmarks are found at the border of putative modules (like sutures of skull bones) and it is difficult to define the modules (separate bone shapes) without re-using landmarks in separate modules.  As Dean pointed out, this is a limitation, but one might argue that it isn’t, if Cardini’s (2019) approach is used?

Tests of modularity basically involve constructing a covariance matrix and partitioning it into symmetric blocks (covariances within modules) and asymmetric blocks (covariance between modules).  Tests statistics either focus on the asymmetric blocks or the strength of covariation in these blocks relative to within the module blocks.  If the same landmarks — and therefore, their coordinates as variables — are found in separate module blocks, there is a corresponding between-module covariance in the asymmetric block for each variable.  As you know, the correlation between a variable and itself is perfectly 1.  Populating this between-module block with covariances of perfectly correlated variables will inflate the correlation between modules, thus inflating the apparent integration (and potentially reducing the strength of modularity).  So even if this could be done by manipulating two.b.pls for a test of integration, it would be a spurious result.  Luckily this is not something that can be as easily finagled with modularity.test, since only one matrix or array is input (one would have to duplicate landmarks to make it work).

But what if one performed separate GPAs on modules, both containing some of the same landmarks, like two separate skull bones sharing a suture?  Now the correlations between them would not be perfectly 1, because the variables are no longer the same even if they are coordinates for the same landmarks.  With several landmarks — say 3 or 4 along the same suture line — there would still be high correlation between the same landmarks in separate modules, as well as those 3-4 landmarks within modules, as well as all of the possible pairs of 3 or 4 landmarks between modules.  This is to say, one still produces a spurious result, but now with the addition of actually altering the real spatial covariances of landmarks on the skull (as found between the contrived modules) with their artificial duplication.  To put it bluntly, this is asinine.

But is it okay then to perform separate GPAs as long as the modules do not contain the same landmarks?  No!  No!  No!  The principle is the same.  One is artificially altering the (presumptively) real covariances that exist between landmarks because of their real spatial locations.  The skull bones cannot be disassembled from the skull if one is evaluating the modularity or integration of putative skull modules, if the skull morphology as defined by the netire configuration is to mean anything.

I implore people to not do separate GPAs and if you feel compelled by reviewers of your manuscript to add that analysis, maybe consider pulling this email from the archives as a rebuttal.  Madlen’s question offers a perfect illustration of why tests of modularity and integration with GM data should not use separate GPAs.  That the modules copuld include the same anatomical references points and in the process their true spatial covariances would be rendered meaningless if a far larger problem than performing separate GPAs could solve.

Madlen, if I were in your shoes, I would take the two modules and make them three: the two previous modules without the shared landmarks and one module for the landmarks they share.  If nothing else, you can learn how integrated these landmarks are with either module.

Cheers!
Mike
